evidence.quote: It begins at Interstate 90 (I-90) in St. Regis and ends at MT 200 near Paradise.

evidence.claim: Montana Highway 135 follows the Clark Fork through Lolo National Forest for 21.5 miles, linking I-90 at St. Regis with MT 200 near Paradise.
evidence.quote: Montana Highway 135 (MT 135) is a 21.5-mile-long (34.6 km) state highway in western Montana.  It begins at Interstate 90 (I-90) in St. Regis and ends at MT 200 near Paradise. The highway runs along the bank of the Clark Fork River and through Lolo National Forest.

evidence.claim: Visit Montana calls this the St. Regis-Paradise Scenic Byway and highlights the change from open, rolling flats to steep canyon walls.
evidence.quote: Follow the St. Regis-Paradise Scenic Byway as it winds through Lolo National Forest, taking you through varying terrain, from spacious, rolling flats to steep canyon walls.

evidence.claim: Road and railway initially share the northern bank of the river.
evidence.quote: along the northern bank of the Clark Fork River.  A line of the Montana Rail Link railroad runs parallel to the highway.

evidence.claim: From 1960 to 1978, a secondary route followed the alignment now used by MT 135.
evidence.quote: From 1960 to 1978, a secondary route ran on the modern route of MT 135.

evidence.claim: It connected U.S. 10 with U.S. 10A, later MT 200, and included a toll-ferry crossing of the Clark Fork.
evidence.quote: It was a connection between US 10 and US 10A and later Montana Highway 200. There was a toll ferry cross the Clark Fork River.

evidence.claim: Leaving St. Regis, the highway heads north and northeast along the river.
evidence.quote: From there, the highway heads to the north and northeast through Lolo National Forest and along the northern bank of the Clark Fork River.

evidence.claim: Near the midpoint, it crosses the Clark Fork and passes beneath the railroad, putting road and tracks on opposite banks.
evidence.quote: Near its midpoint, MT 135 crosses the river and passes beneath the railroad; from there, the road and railroad run along opposite banks of the river.

evidence.claim: The bends straighten near Quinn, and the highway leaves the national forest before meeting MT 200 a couple of miles east of Paradise.
evidence.quote: near Quinn, the river and road straighten.  Just before the highway ends, it exits Lolo National Forest.  The highway ends a couple miles east of Paradise at MT 200.

evidence.claim: Two rivers meet at St. Regis: the St. Regis River joins the Clark Fork here.
evidence.quote: St. Regis is at the confluence of the St. Regis River and the Clark Fork.

evidence.claim: The town takes its name from the St. Regis River, which Pierre-Jean De Smet named for a fellow Jesuit priest.
evidence.quote: He named the river, after which the town takes its name, after a fellow Jesuit priest.

evidence.claim: The post office opened in 1896, and the Northern Pacific Railway built through town in the early 1900s, boosting the local economy.
evidence.quote:
The post office opened in 1896.
The Northern Pacific Railway built a railroad through the town in the early 1900's, boosting the economy.

evidence.claim: MT 135 begins at I-90 and soon meets the former U.S. Highway 10 at a four-way stop.
evidence.quote: MT 135 begins in St. Regis at exit 33 along I-90.  Almost immediately, it comes to a four-way stop where it intersects the former U.S. Highway 10.

evidence.claim: Near the midpoint of MT 135, the road crosses the Clark Fork and passes beneath the railroad.

evidence.claim: Until this crossing, road and tracks have run together along the northern bank.

evidence.claim: Paradise was a place to reset a railroad watch: crews changed from Mountain to Pacific time here.
evidence.quote: It was also the place where railroaders would change their watches from Mountain to Pacific time.

evidence.claim: The community began in 1883 when the Northern Pacific Railroad selected it as a division point.
evidence.quote: The community began in 1883, when the Northern Pacific Railroad chose the site as a division point.
